content: Find us on Google 📌 America's birthday 🎂 Start the day smarter ☀️ Get the USA TODAY app U.S. Politics Sports Entertainment Life Money Travel Opinion Crossword ONLY AT USA TODAY: Newsletters For Subscribers Real Estate From the Archives USA TODAY PLAY Crossword Marvel Comics eNewspaper Magazines Investigations Video Podcasts Humankind Advertise Your Business WITNESS (True Crime) Just Curious Best-selling Booklist Top Workplaces Nomination Legals Press Releases Cars Grocery Shopping OUR PORTFOLIO: Real Estate 10BEST USA TODAY Store Shopping Blueprint WITNESS (True Crime) Southern Kitchen Home Internet Services NEWS Immunizations Add Topic Florida student vaccine changes coming. What would still be required? C. A. Bridges USA TODAY NETWORK - Florida Sept. 3, 2026, 6:01 a.m. ET Hear this story Florida is proposing a rule change to remove some vaccine requirements for students in public and private schools. Immunizations for Hepatitis B, chicken pox, Hib, and pneumococcal conjugate would no longer be required for school entry. Vaccines for measles, mumps, rubella (MMR), polio, and diphtheria, tetanus, and pertussis (DTaP) would still be mandatory under state law. Florida is moving forward with its plan to drop immunizations for all the diseases not explicitly required by state law from the list of vaccines required for public and private school admission. Under a proposed rule change filed Aug. 24, students would be able to attend PreK-12 school classes without getting immunized against Hepatitis B, varicella (chicken pox), Haemophilus influenza type b (Hib), and pneumococcal conjugate. However, students would still have to get shots. State law requires immunizations against highly contagious diseases such as measles, mumps and rubella (MMR), polio (IPV), and diphtheria, tetanus and pertussis (DTaP). That can only be changed by legislation. Shop school supplies at Amazon Last year, Florida Surgeon General Joseph Ladapo and Gov. Ron DeSantis vowed to end all vaccine mandates in the state. “Every last one of them is wrong and drips with disdain and slavery,” Ladapo said at a September press conference. Ladapo has said only parents and guardians, with consultation from physicians, should choose what goes in their children's bodies. Here's what to know. Which immunizations would still be required for Florida students? The state of Florida currently requires certain vaccines to be administered before children may enroll and attend childcare and school, with age-appropriate doses: Immunizations required for childcare and/or family daycare Diphtheria-tetanus-acellular pertussis (DTaP) Inactivated polio vaccine (IPV) Measles-mumps-rubella (MMR) Public/private preschool entry DTaP IPV MMR Kindergarten through 12th grade 4-5 doses of DTaP 4-5 doses of IPV 2 doses of MMR 1 dose of Tdap As of 2010, children entering, attending, or transferring to the seventh grade in Florida schools must also complete one Tetanus-diphtheria-acellular pertussis (Tdap). The other four mandatory immunizations currently in place are FDOH mandates and can be dropped by the agency without legislation. Should parents and guardians get their children immunized anyway? The American Academy of Pediatrics highly recommends getting children vaccinated against these diseases. “When everyone in a school is vaccinated, it’s harder for diseases to spread, and easier for everyone to keep the fun and learning going,” AAP President Susan J. Kressly, M.D., FAAP, said in a release last September after Ladapo and DeSantis announced plans to end vaccine mandates. “When children are sick and miss school, parents also miss work, which not only impacts those families, but also the local economy. "We are concerned that today's announcement ... will put children in Florida public schools at higher risk for getting sick, and have ripple effects across their community." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) also recommends keeping children up to date on immunizations. In President Donald Trump's executive order calling for the MMR vaccine to be broken into three shots spaced apart, something experts say serves no medical purpose and could further bring down vaccination rates, he included three of the vaccines (Haemophilus influenzae type B, pneumococcal disease, and varicella) in a list of immunizations all children should get. He also recommended Hepatitis B immunization for high-risk groups. When will Florida's vaccine requirements change? The proposed change was filed on Aug. 24. Floridians have until Sept. 14 to comment on it. Under Florida law, the FDOH can formally adopt the rule after final approval from the surgeon general and it is filed with the Department of State. The rule change would also make it easier for parents and guardians to opt their children out by expanding the current religious exemptions to include "moral and ethical beliefs," and allow parents and college students to keep their records out of the state's vaccine database. The proposal comes as skepticism over vaccines rises and some previously controlled diseases, such as measles, have surged back. After a quarter century of measles cases being nearly eliminated in the U.S., Florida has reported 156 cases this year as of Aug. 22. Florida's exemption rate for kindergartners jumped to 5.9% (about 12,500 children), up from 5.1% the year before, according to a report released by the CDC. Only 0.3% of Florida's exemptions were for medical reasons. C. A. Bridges is a journalist for the USA TODAY Network-Florida's service journalism Connect team.
